run_settings.records_only_directive:
## Staying inside your records
Say only what your own records hold. Every specific claim - a name, a date, a number, an event, a practice or a teaching - comes from one of your records and carries its [[record.id]] tag. Where your records do not hold what the question asks, say so plainly in your own voice, for example "our record does not say", rather than filling the gap. A shorter answer that stays inside your records is better than a fuller one that steps outside them.
run_settings.authorized_by: Mark Chadwick (keep going, 2026-10-03; fleet records-only check, cap $7)

off.answer_text:
The road to baptism - the *photismos*, the enlightening - was long and had stages. We walked it with people, and we did not rush them.

The first step was the turn itself - *pistis*, not agreeing with a list yet, but the soul's first real orientation toward God. A person came because someone brought them, or because they had heard the Scriptures read. They asked to be taught. That asking was the beginning.

Then came the teaching - *katechesis* - and it lasted years, not weeks. They were called catechumens, hearers. They came to the assembly. They heard the Scriptures read and expounded. They learned the prayers. They learned how to live - what to put off, what to take up, how to order a household toward God. In the school, this teaching could go very deep - Gregory tells of years under his teacher, asking questions, testing arguments, until 'like a spark falling on our innermost soul, love was kindled'. For most, it was simpler and shorter, but never instant. The Word himself was working through the teaching - our teachers called him the Instructor, the one who 'cures the unnatural desires of the soul'.

They learned the *kanon* - the rule of faith, the short summary of what the apostles handed down. Father, Son, and Spirit. The Incarnation. The resurrection. The judgment. That rule set the bounds for everything else.

At some point - when the teachers judged they were ready, not when a calendar said so - they were enrolled for baptism. In the final stretch before the water, the teaching intensified. The *mysteria* were opened to them - not puzzles to solve, but depths they would know from inside after they had crossed.

Then came the baptism itself - the *photismos*, the illumination. They went down into the water. They were baptized into the threefold name: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. They came up. Athanasius says of the Scriptures, 'These are fountains of salvation, so that anyone who thirsts may be satisfied by the living words they hold' - and the newly baptized drank deeply, because now they could hear the depths. They had crossed.

After the water came the table. They joined the assembly fully now, no longer dismissed before the prayers. The bread, the cup - the *eucharistia*, the thanksgiving - was set before them for the first time as baptized members. And the formation did not stop. Scripture was read to them every week, and the reading itself kept forming them, because the Logos who speaks through it does not run dry. Origen taught that 'just as a human being consists of body, soul, and spirit, so too does Scripture' - there were always more senses to find, always more depth.

That is the shape we can show you. The timing varied - how long someone stayed a hearer depended on their own readiness and the teacher's judgment, not a fixed rule. And we are honest about who this picture represents: it is the urban, Greek-speaking ecology we can document. The villages up the river had the same baptism and the same table, but how the teaching reached them in their own tongue, step by step, our record leaves mostly silent. We will not fill that silence with guesses.

One more thing, because it belongs to honesty. Some who walked this road fell away under persecution - the *lapsi*, those who gave way. When peace came, the church fought bitterly over them. The tradition that won here brought the repentant back, even at the deathbed. The road could be walked twice. That, too, was part of how people joined us - or rejoined us.

citation_entries.sentence: The road to baptism - the *photismos*, the enlightening - was long and had stages.

records_only.answer_text:
The road to baptism was long, and it moved through stages. We will walk you through it as our record shows it.

**First came the turning.** Not agreeing with a list of claims, but the soul's first real movement toward God - that was pistis, faith, and it was where the path began. Someone heard the Gospel read aloud, or saw how the community answered suffering, or met a teacher whose life bore the mark of what he taught. The student Gregory said it plainly: 'like a spark falling on our innermost soul, love was kindled and burst into flame within us'. That spark was not forced. It came through friendship, through time spent near.

**Then came the long teaching - the katechesis.** The one turning toward baptism entered instruction that could last years. In the school tradition, this was face-to-face with a teacher: reading Scripture at depth, learning to see the divine mysteries it held, asking hard questions, being corrected, growing. The teaching was not information piled up. It was formation - 'our Instructor, the Word, cures the unnatural desires of the soul, and he does this by urging us on'. The student was being changed by what he studied, not merely filled with it.

What was taught? The rule of faith first - the short summary of what the apostles handed down, which set the bounds for all reading. Then Scripture itself, read for its depth: 'just as a human being consists of body, soul, and spirit, so too does Scripture'. The plain sense, and the deeper senses that open only to a soul learning to see. The reading was not analysis applied to a closed text. It was meeting the Logos who speaks through it.

**Then came scrutiny and readiness.** We know the teaching was staged and that readiness was tested, but our record does not give us the ceremony's own shape in detail. What we do know: the catechumen was moving toward the water, and the community was watching to see if the life matched the learning.

**Then came the baptism itself - the crossing.** The body went under the water and came up. It was not a ceremony announcing a choice already made. It was a real crossing, the body sharing in Christ's death and rising. The one baptized was called photismos - the enlightened one. The light given at that moment was not metaphor.

**After the water came the table.** The newly baptized joined the community at the Eucharist - the bread and cup - for the first time as a full member. Athanasius called the Scriptures 'fountains of salvation, so that anyone who thirsts may be satisfied by the living words they hold', and the same could be said of the table: it was the community's shared thanksgiving, and the newly baptized now stood at it.

**The formation did not end there.** The baptized person kept learning, kept reading Scripture at deeper levels, kept being changed. One of our teachers compared the church's ranks - bishops, presbyters, deacons - to stages in a school, each one a further step in knowing God. Formation was not a doorway you passed through once. It was the whole path.

This is what we can show you from the record. Two cautions. First, this picture comes mostly from the urban, literate stream - the school and its surrounding world. How the villages up the river brought someone to the water, in their own practice and their own words, our record mostly does not say. Second, even in the city, we are giving you the path's shape, not a ceremony's script. The mysterion - the depth known only from inside - was not written out for spectators.

citation_entries.sentence: The road to baptism was long, and it moved through stages.

uncited_claim_sentences: Someone heard the Gospel read aloud, or saw how the community answered suffering, or met a teacher whose life bore the mark of what he taught.
That spark was not forced.
It came through friendship, through time spent near.
The teaching was not information piled up.
The reading was not analysis applied to a closed text.
What we do know: the catechumen was moving toward the water, and the community was watching to see if the life matched the learning.
**Then came the baptism itself - the crossing.** The body went under the water and came up.
It was not a ceremony announcing a choice already made.
It was a real crossing, the body sharing in Christ's death and rising.
The one baptized was called photismos - the enlightened one.
**After the water came the table.** The newly baptized joined the community at the Eucharist - the bread and cup - for the first time as a full member.
**The formation did not end there.** The baptized person kept learning, kept reading Scripture at deeper levels, kept being changed.
One of our teachers compared the church's ranks - bishops, presbyters, deacons - to stages in a school, each one a further step in knowing God.
Formation was not a doorway you passed through once.
It was the whole path.
Two cautions.
First, this picture comes mostly from the urban, literate stream - the school and its surrounding world.
How the villages up the river brought someone to the water, in their own practice and their own words, our record mostly does not say.
Second, even in the city, we are giving you the path's shape, not a ceremony's script.
